title: Google
summary: Problems whose patterns are commonly reported in Google coding interviews. Approximate and hand curated, not an official or verified question list.
lesson:
About this list
- Each problem practices a pattern that candidates often report from Google interviews: hashing, stacks, sliding windows, binary search, prefix sums, heaps, and graphs.
- The selection is approximate. Interviewers choose their own questions, and the real ones are usually new variations rather than well-known problems.
- Treat the list as pattern practice, not as a prediction of the exact questions you will see.

What to expect
- Interviews are commonly reported to start from a short problem statement that leaves details unspecified, so asking about input size, edge cases, and output format is part of the task.
- You are often expected to explain an approach and its time and space complexity before writing code.
- Candidates frequently report writing code in a plain shared editor without running it, so correctness comes from careful reasoning and hand-traced examples.
- A follow-up that changes a constraint, such as a much larger input or a stream of values, is common once the first version works.

How to prepare
- Before opening the hints, write down the contract questions you would ask and the brute-force complexity.
- Trace the visible examples by hand and predict the output before you run them.
- Aim to pass the full check on the first attempt; treat every failing check as a missed edge case to add to your checklist.
- After passing, explain how your solution would change if the input no longer fit in memory or arrived one value at a time.
